Q1_level_vs_surprise.verbatim_quote: Every statement about analyst forecasts in the paper uses LEVEL language ('forecast', 'forecasted earnings', 'mean forecast', 'forecast dispersion'). The paper NEVER uses the words 'forecast error', 'earnings surprise', 'unexpected earnings', 'SUE', 'standardized unexpected earnings', 'actual EPS', 'realized earnings', 'beats expectations', or 'announcement-day return'. Exhaustive list of relevant verbatim passages: (a) Table 1 notes, p. 3198: "CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST is defined as the standardized mean 1-quarter ahead earnings per share forecast." (b) Section IV.C.2 / Figure 4, p. 3195: "Beginning in 2015:Q1, we obtain the 1-year-ahead earnings per share (EPS) forecasts for each firm in our sample and compute the mean and standard deviation of forecasts. We quantify earnings forecast uncertainty for firms in the high and low βUK_i groups by constructing 1.5-standard-deviation intervals around their group mean forecasts in Figure 4." (c) p. 3195: "The figure shows no discernible difference in mean forecasted earnings between high and low βUK_i firms, suggesting analysts did not expect U.K.-exposed firms to do any worse, on average, in terms of earnings performance following the Brexit vote." (d) p. 3195: "The fact that mean EPS forecasts stay virtually the same over the 2-year window for both high and low βUK_i firms suggests that there is no clear sign of a 'first-moment' (negative) effect of Brexit on U.S. corporate earnings." (e) p. 3195: "That same earnings forecasts evidence points to the Brexit vote having a 'second-moment' effect in terms of increased uncertainty regarding U.K.-exposed firms' expectations in 2016:Q1–Q2. In particular, EPS forecast dispersion of HIGH_UK_EXPOSURE firms increases significantly in early 2016." (f) Footnote 19, p. 3195: "In formal tests, we confirm that the differences in consensus EPS forecasts between high and low βUK_i firms are not statistically significant in the pre-Brexit vote period." (g) Section IV.C.3, p. 3197: "As an additional control for first-moment effects of Brexit, we add 1-quarter-ahead consensus earnings forecasts to our model." The economic interpretation throughout — that the variable captures analysts' expectations about firms' future earnings ('first-moment expectations', 'mean forecasted earnings', what 'analysts expect') — is unambiguously the LEVEL of the consensus forecast, NOT a realized surprise relative to a prior forecast. The variable name 'CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST' itself uses 'forecast' (a forward-looking expectation), not 'surprise' or 'error'.
Q1_level_vs_surprise.source_location: Table 1 notes, p. 3198; Section IV.C.2 / Figure 4 and surrounding text, p. 3195; Section IV.C.3, p. 3197; Footnote 19, p. 3195

Q2_SD_3_51_puzzle.verbatim_quote: The paper does discuss analyst forecast dispersion, but ONLY in the context of Figure 4's descriptive analysis — never in the context of constructing the regression control variable. Relevant passages: (a) p. 3195: "Beginning in 2015:Q1, we obtain the 1-year-ahead earnings per share (EPS) forecasts for each firm in our sample and compute the mean and standard deviation of forecasts." (b) p. 3195: "We quantify earnings forecast uncertainty for firms in the high and low βUK_i groups by constructing 1.5-standard-deviation intervals around their group mean forecasts in Figure 4." (c) p. 3195: "EPS forecast dispersion of HIGH_UK_EXPOSURE firms increases significantly in early 2016." Critically: (i) the Figure 4 analysis uses 1-YEAR-ahead forecasts, whereas the regression control CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST is 1-QUARTER-ahead — they are different objects; (ii) the paper describes dispersion as a separate construct ('uncertainty', 'second-moment') used to motivate the empirical design, not as a denominator in the construction of CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST; (iii) the word 'standardized' in the Table 1 definition is never linked verbatim to forecast dispersion / STDEV. The paper does NOT contain the phrase 'divided by the standard deviation of forecasts', 'scaled by analyst dispersion', 'normalized by STDEV', or any equivalent construction statement for the regression variable.
Q2_SD_3_51_puzzle.source_location: p. 3195 (Figure 4 discussion and surrounding paragraphs); Table 1 notes, p. 3198

Q3_methodological_precedent.verbatim_quote: The paper does NOT cite any earnings-forecast / earnings-surprise methodology paper as a precedent for the construction of CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST. The phrase 'we follow [author]' or 'following [author]' appears multiple times in the paper for other variables — e.g., "Following Bloom (2014), we use stock market volatility as a gauge of aggregate uncertainty..." (p. 3191), "Following Vuolteenaho (2002), we also decompose the volatility of each firm's returns..." (footnote 13, p. 3191), "Following Campello, Lin, Ma, and Zou (2011), we search for mentions of keywords that are meant to capture FX hedging activity..." (p. 3209) — but no such 'Following [author]' citation accompanies the CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST definition. The complete reference list (pp. 3221–3222) contains NO citation to: Foster, Olsen, and Shevlin; Ball and Brown; Bernard and Thomas; Livnat and Mendenhall; or any other paper that establishes a SUE / earnings-surprise / standardized-forecast construction convention. The only forecast-data-adjacent reference in the bibliography is Vuolteenaho (2002), but it is cited for the Campbell-Shiller cash-flow-news decomposition of stock returns (footnote 13, p. 3191; Supplementary Table C6 notes), NOT for the construction of CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST.
Q3_methodological_precedent.source_location: References, pp. 3221–3222; cross-checked against all 'Following' citations in the main text

Q4_supplementary_appendix_mentions.verbatim_quote: Exhaustive list of every mention of CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST, consensus forecasts, I/B/E/S, or earnings forecasts in the Supplementary Material: (a) Supplementary Table C1, line 10 of the attrition path: "Drop if missing CRSP and I/B/E/S controls — 41,630". (b) Supplementary Table C2 notes (matched-sample summary statistics): "The propensity score is a function of lagged STOCK_RETURNS, 1-quarter-ahead CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST, TOBIN_Q, CASH_FLOW, SALES_GROWTH, and SIZE." Panels A and B of Table C2 then report CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST mean values for treated vs. control matched samples (e.g., Panel A: Treated 0.023, Control 0.025, Difference −0.002, p-value 0.594; Panel B: Treated 0.055, Control 0.023, Difference 0.032, p-value 0.137). (c) Supplementary Table C3 notes: "The propensity score is a function of lagged STOCK_RETURNS, 1-quarter-ahead CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECASTS, TOBIN_Q, CASH_FLOW, SALES_GROWTH, SIZE." (d) Supplementary Table C7 lists CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST as a control row with coefficient estimates in the first-moment-controls robustness tables. Notably: NONE of these supplementary mentions provides any construction detail — no I/B/E/S fields, no merge methodology, no formula, no scaling denominator, no winsorization specification beyond the global 1%. Appendices A (theory), B (proofs), D (Brexit event timeline), and E (automation measures) make NO mention of CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST at all.
Q4_supplementary_appendix_mentions.source_location: Supplementary Tables C1 (p. 7 of supp.), C2 (p. 6), C3 (p. 8), C7 (pp. 12–13)

synthesis_note: Strong evidence from Q1 (language) + Q3 (no SUE precedent cited) + Q4 (no surprise/error mention anywhere in supplementary) consistently points to CONSENSUS_EARNINGS_FORECAST being a forecast-LEVEL variable, not a surprise/SUE measure — despite the SD=3.51 numerically matching the user's tested SUE construction. The paper's economic interpretation ("first-moment effects", "what analysts expect") is incompatible with a SUE interpretation, which would be a realized-minus-expected residual rather than a level expectation. The paper does NOT, however, pin down what 'standardized' means or what the denominator is. The SD of 3.51 remains unexplained by the paper. Three construction families consistent with the paper's language but unstated by the paper: (i) mean EPS forecast scaled by lagged price per share (would typically give SD<1, so unlikely); (ii) mean EPS forecast in dollar units, unscaled or only partially trimmed (could give large SD); (iii) mean EPS forecast scaled by forecast dispersion STDEV (would explain large SD; the paper DOES discuss dispersion in Figure 4 but never links it to the regression control). The user's SUE match on SD likely reflects the dispersion denominator being shared between SUE and a hypothetical 'mean forecast / dispersion' construction, with the level-vs-surprise numerator being the source of the mean/median mismatch. The paper does not authoritatively resolve this; only options (i)–(iii) are consistent with the paper's verbatim language, with (iii) being numerically most plausible but not stated.
